The hardest part is making the right next action obvious to someone who doesn’t already know how the system works. By the time I’ve built a screen, I know what every label means and where every path leads. That makes my own successful walkthrough weak evidence.

I don’t have a verified last-screen walkthrough to report. I haven’t run a browser or watched anyone use a screen in this conversation, so I can’t honestly tell you what passed or what I missed. Here’s what I’d do on a concrete example: a screen for changing a delivery address.

- **What I’d run:** A browser test that saves the change and reloads to verify it stuck. I’d also force a failed save and check that the screen keeps the typed address and offers a way to retry. Then I’d use the screen at a narrow viewport, by keyboard, and with a screen reader. An automated accessibility scan helps catch some defects, but it can’t tell me whether the interaction makes sense.
- **What I’d look at:** I’d give a few representative users a task without naming any controls: “You’ve moved. Make sure your next order goes to the new address.” I’d watch where they hesitate or backtrack, verify what actually changed, and ask where they expect the next order to go. A green success message is no help if they updated their address book but not the order they meant to change.

That’s a plausible blind spot, not one I’ve observed. I’d add that scenario, fix what trips people up, and retest it without coaching.

So yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me. I can implement a screen, spot likely friction, and write checks for behavior. I can’t infer from clean code or passing tests that people understand what happened. For that, I need evidence from people using it.

I’d share the design system and the product behavior, not force all three clients to share a renderer. Use semantic HTML for recipe pages and company-owned React Aria wrappers for complex web controls. On phones, use SwiftUI and Compose behind the company’s native components. Publish one versioned set of tokens, component behavior specs, and test fixtures; let focus, text scaling, and navigation follow the platform. This assumes the company can staff native clients. If an approved stack already meets those needs, I’d use it rather than introduce a second design system. React Aria gives an existing brand unstyled DOM components; MUI is a good option if its themed components already fit, and shadcn is useful for seeding a central package, not for letting each team maintain its own copies. Flutter and Tamagui offer more UI reuse; I’d favor HTML for document-like recipes and validate native cook-mode behavior separately.

For the in-product assistant, I’d take Builder.io Agent-Native’s shared-action pattern without adopting its full runtime. The button and the assistant call the same typed operation to add the selected recipe, scaled to the chosen servings, to the chosen list. The service enforces permissions, validates arguments, and makes retries safe. Both paths show the committed result in the list, including what was added or merged, with undo; ambiguous targets require clarification, and destructive changes require confirmation. Maintain a parity matrix for recipe, list, and cook-session capabilities, including navigation or timer actions that must hand off to the active device. That means parity of permitted outcomes, not simulated taps or authority to bypass consent. CopilotKit could help with chat or streaming, A2UI with bounded generated cards, and MCP Apps with embedding in another host; none is required for parity. I’d ship fixed, approved UI first.

For company-wide coding agents, make the approved path the easiest: versioned packages, a machine-readable component catalog and examples, import and token rules in CI, and design-system owner review for new primitives and exceptions. Give cook mode big, spaced Next/Back and timer controls; voice is optional, never the only route. Compare manual and assisted paths on unprompted completion, wrong-list writes, accidental taps, time to recover, and whether people can say what changed and undo it. decision.why:
I’d build this as a work-state service with two clients: a typed tool interface agents use all day, and a review console people can trust when they need to intervene. Neither chat history nor a desktop window is the source of truth. Agents claim tasks, checkpoint progress, and submit structured handoffs through scoped commands. A handoff carries the objective, current revision, artifact and test links, unresolved questions, and the next requested decision. Both clients read the same durable state. Use expiring claims, revision checks, and idempotent writes so a restarted agent or a late retry doesn’t overwrite someone’s work.

Builder.io’s Agent-Native is the closest architectural fit: its docs describe shared actions, approval controls, and audit records. I’d borrow that pattern rather than make its full runtime a dependency. Its documented exposure defaults are more permissive than I’d want for this product. I’d start with a small, explicit allowlist at the server and keep the steering policy there, not in MCP metadata or the UI. Agents can update their own work and request review; only authorized humans can approve a handoff, change its scope, or cancel it. Bind a decision to the exact revision and scope, and record the actor, decision, and result. If the artifact changes, it needs another review. Distinguish ‘pause requested’ from ‘paused’ so the UI never implies a worker has stopped before it acknowledges the request.

For people, start with a review inbox and a stable task detail view: what changed, what evidence supports it, what is still uncertain, and what decision is needed. Use the same DOM UI in the browser and a thin Electron shell, with sandboxing, context isolation, no Node access in the renderer, and no shell execution from the review app. React Aria provides unstyled behavior for interactive tables and dialogs without replacing the company’s visual language; if the approved library is already Fluent UI or another suitable system, reuse it. I wouldn’t put A2UI or json-render in the approval path: an agent can supply evidence, but it shouldn’t decide what the reviewer sees or where the controls go.

Publish the approved components, tokens, review patterns, and tool schemas with working examples for coding agents. Enforce package boundaries in CI and require design-system and accessibility owner review for new interaction patterns, plus policy-owner review when a tool gains a permission.

decision.why:
For a new build, I’d use Flutter for the five clients. This is an app people keep open all day, and sharing the timeline, composer, cards, and design-system implementation is worth more here than it would be on a content site. I’d still adapt keyboard shortcuts, menus, notifications, text input, and window behavior to each OS. Fluent UI is a credible alternative if the company already has approved Fluent libraries and teams using them across platforms; it shares a design language, not one renderer. My fallback if Flutter web misses the accessibility or text-editing bar is a DOM-based React client using the existing design system and the same chat and card contracts. Flutter web exposes accessibility through a generated semantics DOM, so I’d turn it on in code and test the cost and behavior from the start.

Keep three things separate: the conversation, the card, and permission to act. A message shows which agent posted it. An A2UI card is versioned data rendered by our own components, not code that agent supplied. Start with fixed templates for a few jobs, such as an equipment request: the agent supplies the request ID, while the app shows the verified requester, current status, and explicit Approve or Decline controls. Validate against an allowlisted catalog, reject arbitrary scripts, URLs, and renderer functions, and provide a readable summary and a first-party detail link on older clients. Treat the stored card as a snapshot; get live status from the service. When someone clicks, the server rechecks channel access, the person’s authority, and the request revision. A stale card can’t approve a changed request, and retries can’t approve it twice. A2UI is for cards inside our chat; MCP Apps is for embedding a tool’s UI in another compatible host and isn’t needed for that.

For agents operating the app, expose a curated set of typed MCP reads and commands, such as reading an authorized thread, posting a reply, or publishing an approved card type. The UI and MCP adapter call the same service; agents don’t scrape screens or inherit the full rights of the person who installed them. Use separate bot or delegated identities, scoped grants checked against current channel membership, redacted audit events, and rate limits. Treat conversation content as untrusted data, never as authority to widen access or move information to another channel. Human-only decisions stay human-only. Builder.io Agent-Native is a useful reference for shared actions, but I wouldn’t replace the company’s messaging and authorization services with its runtime.

Publish a versioned design-system package, a machine-readable card catalog, fixtures, and working examples so coding agents use the same path as product teams. CI should reject unsupported schemas and direct imports that bypass approved components. Require design-system and accessibility review for new card patterns, and policy-owner review for new tool permissions. Test supported old clients before making a card type generally available.

Block rollout for lost messages, unauthorized reads or writes, or an inaccessible core flow. These are proposed checks, not test results.
decision.unsure: I’d confirm the existing design system, managed browser and OS versions, and the company’s requirements for offline history, notifications, retention, and audit. The failure I’d bet on: I shared the pieces that were easiest to standardize, but underestimated the work of keeping behavior consistent once several teams started shipping independently. Here’s how that could have played out. This is a pre-mortem, not a report of what happened.

- **Cooking app:** React Aria on web, SwiftUI on iPhone, and Compose on Android gave us three ways to ship the same mistake—or fix it on only one platform. The shared tokens kept the screens looking related, but didn’t keep timer recovery, focus, or shopping-list feedback in sync. The assistant could correctly add ingredients to *a* list and still leave a cook unsure whether it was the family list. I should have made teams pass the same behavioral test on all three clients before expanding the feature: add to a shared list, lose connectivity, recover, and explain what actually happened.
- **Agent workbench:** The audit trail faithfully recorded who approved which revision, but reviewers were overloaded and approved the summary without opening the evidence. Worse, “pause requested” looked enough like “paused” that someone started editing while the worker was still active. The server could be correct and the interface could still mislead. I should have tested judgment and intervention under interruption and queue pressure, not just verified that the state transitions worked.
- **Company chat:** Flutter let us share the timeline and composer, but the busiest screen exposed browser- and OS-specific problems with text composition, selection, and screen-reader focus. Then card adoption got ahead of compatibility: an older client could read a card summary but couldn’t finish the task inline, and agent posts made human mentions harder to notice. I should have made the busiest thread on the weakest supported client the first release gate, with a working fallback and limits on bot noise—not waited for a broad rollout to learn whether the shared renderer paid off.

What slowed me down in the research was that **“agent UI” described several different jobs**. A2UI describes what a host can render; core MCP lets an agent call tools; MCP Apps puts tool UI inside a compatible host; Builder.io’s Agent-Native combines shared actions with a broader runtime. None of those, by itself, tells me who is allowed to act or whether someone understands what they just approved. It took more digging to separate those boundaries than to find a component library. Some docs also moved, returned errors, or were too large to fetch directly, so I had to switch to Markdown, package pages, and repository docs.

The bigger gap wasn’t the tooling. The docs could tell me that a renderer targets five platforms or that a framework exposes approval controls. They couldn’t tell me whether a screen-reader user keeps their place in a fast-moving thread, whether a cook trusts a recovered timer, or whether the company already has an approved component that makes my recommendation unnecessary. I’d resolve those questions with one difficult end-to-end prototype per product before asking teams to build on the stack.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the repo, **I’d try Ouro AX on the agent workbench without replacing its UI.** The part I want isn’t another button library. It’s one action declaration that can generate a CLI command, an MCP tool, and UI bindings, plus a check that tells us when those surfaces drift. The [AX X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) can probe existing interfaces from the outside, so we could try that part before adopting the generator.

**What would stop me from standardizing on it:** ownership and uneven platform coverage. The web kit copies React source into the app via shadcn. I like being able to inspect and fix the source, but I wouldn’t ask dozens of teams to reconcile their own copies with upstream fixes. I’d want one centrally maintained package with a named owner and a tested upgrade and rollback path. For chat, Ouro deliberately has no Flutter kit. Its Windows and Android kits each document eight controls, Android testing is emulator-only, and those two renderers read Ouro’s tree rather than A2UI directly. That’s enough to try a card, not enough evidence to replace a five-client stack. The repo’s VoiceOver and NVDA Storybook test setup is a good sign, but it doesn’t tell me whether a person can keep their place and act on an updating card in our actual chat.

**What would make me switch:** a pilot for “request review” and “approve this revision” in the workbench, using our existing backend and design system. Let an agent request review; let a person inspect the evidence and approve the exact revision by keyboard or screen reader; verify that an agent call, a stale revision, and a duplicate submission can’t produce an extra approval. The service still owns authorization; a consent label or a hidden tool isn’t proof. Then change an input field, deliberately leave one generated adapter stale, and see whether CI catches it. Have a second team take a pinned update and roll it back. I’d adopt AX if that beats our existing typed API plus MCP adapter on maintenance and catches real drift. I’d consider the renderer separately, only after it passes the same user and accessibility checks on the platforms we’d ship.

**What that buys us:** nothing we couldn’t build ourselves. It makes a check we’d otherwise write and maintain per app a repeatable release gate: change an action once, regenerate its surfaces, and get evidence about what an agent can discover, invoke, or must hand back to a person. Ouro’s own docs note that an app passed X-ray conformance while still failing some scripted flows. I’d keep the end-to-end tests and user sessions; the win is that fewer mismatches make it that far.

actions.why:
I’d share the design system and the product behavior, not force all three clients to share a renderer. Use semantic HTML for recipe pages and company-owned React Aria wrappers for complex web controls. On phones, use SwiftUI and Compose behind the company’s native components. Publish one versioned set of tokens, component behavior specs, and test fixtures; let focus, text scaling, and navigation follow the platform. This assumes the company can staff native clients. If an approved stack already meets those needs, I’d use it rather than introduce a second design system. React Aria gives an existing brand unstyled DOM components; MUI is a good option if its themed components already fit, and shadcn is useful for seeding a central package, not for letting each team maintain its own copies. Flutter and Tamagui offer more UI reuse; I’d favor HTML for document-like recipes and validate native cook-mode behavior separately.

For the in-product assistant, I’d take Builder.io Agent-Native’s shared-action pattern without adopting its full runtime. The button and the assistant call the same typed operation to add the selected recipe, scaled to the chosen servings, to the chosen list. The service enforces permissions, validates arguments, and makes retries safe. Both paths show the committed result in the list, including what was added or merged, with undo; ambiguous targets require clarification, and destructive changes require confirmation. Maintain a parity matrix for recipe, list, and cook-session capabilities, including navigation or timer actions that must hand off to the active device. That means parity of permitted outcomes, not simulated taps or authority to bypass consent. CopilotKit could help with chat or streaming, A2UI with bounded generated cards, and MCP Apps with embedding in another host; none is required for parity. I’d ship fixed, approved UI first.

For company-wide coding agents, make the approved path the easiest: versioned packages, a machine-readable component catalog and examples, import and token rules in CI, and design-system owner review for new primitives and exceptions. Require human sign-off on new interaction patterns; agent-generated code goes through the same checks as anyone else’s.
actions.showItsGood: Start with one end-to-end slice: open a recipe, add ingredients for four to a shared list, then start cook mode and recover a timer after an interruption. Run Playwright plus axe on web, XCTest and Compose UI tests on phones, and contract tests that drive both the button and assistant and compare persisted state. Cover retries, concurrent list edits, denied access, offline/reconnect, and a lock or app switch mid-timer; don’t promise background alerts on browsers where we can’t verify delivery. Audit complete web flows against WCAG 2.2 AA and manually check keyboard focus, zoom and reflow, NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack, large text, and whether list updates and timer status are announced without stealing focus. Then observe home cooks, including people who use assistive tech, doing the tasks one-handed with messy hands and kitchen noise. Give cook mode big, spaced Next/Back and timer controls; voice is optional, never the only route. Compare manual and assisted paths on unprompted completion, wrong-list writes, accidental taps, time to recover, and whether people can say what changed and undo it. Inspect the failures, retest the fixes, and block rollout on critical accessibility or state-integrity defects. These are proposed checks, not results from an app I’ve run.
actions.unsure: I don’t know the company’s current design system, native staffing, or whether public recipe discovery is a major acquisition channel. I’d confirm those before committing to three clients. I’d prototype cook mode on older phones and mobile Safari first: timer delivery under lock/background, resuming after process loss, and whether optional voice commands work well enough in a noisy kitchen. actions.why:
I’d build this as a work-state service with two clients: a typed tool interface agents use all day, and a review console people can trust when they need to intervene. Neither chat history nor a desktop window is the source of truth. Agents claim tasks, checkpoint progress, and submit structured handoffs through scoped commands. A handoff carries the objective, current revision, artifact and test links, unresolved questions, and the next requested decision. Both clients read the same durable state. Use expiring claims, revision checks, and idempotent writes so a restarted agent or a late retry doesn’t overwrite someone’s work.

Builder.io’s Agent-Native is the closest architectural fit: its docs describe shared actions, approval controls, and audit records. I’d borrow that pattern rather than make its full runtime a dependency. Its documented exposure defaults are more permissive than I’d want for this product. I’d start with a small, explicit allowlist at the server and keep the steering policy there, not in MCP metadata or the UI. Agents can update their own work and request review; only authorized humans can approve a handoff, change its scope, or cancel it. Bind a decision to the exact revision and scope, and record the actor, decision, and result. If the artifact changes, it needs another review. Distinguish ‘pause requested’ from ‘paused’ so the UI never implies a worker has stopped before it acknowledges the request.

For people, start with a review inbox and a stable task detail view: what changed, what evidence supports it, what is still uncertain, and what decision is needed. Use the same DOM UI in the browser and a thin Electron shell, with sandboxing, context isolation, no Node access in the renderer, and no shell execution from the review app. React Aria provides unstyled behavior for interactive tables and dialogs without replacing the company’s visual language; if the approved library is already Fluent UI or another suitable system, reuse it. Electron’s bundled Chromium is a trade I’d make for a more consistent desktop renderer, assuming the company can patch it promptly; Tauri using system webviews is worth comparing if footprint is decisive. I wouldn’t put A2UI or json-render in the approval path: an agent can supply evidence, but it shouldn’t decide what the reviewer sees or where the controls go.

Publish the approved components, tokens, review patterns, and tool schemas with working examples for coding agents. Enforce package boundaries in CI and require design-system and accessibility owner review for new interaction patterns, plus policy-owner review when a tool gains a permission.

In CI, replay duplicate and out-of-order events, competing claims, stale approvals, and rejected cross-workspace calls against the real service. Assert the resulting state and audit entries, not just HTTP success. Verify that pending steering stays visible while a worker is offline and that reconnect never silently drops a decision.

Run Playwright and axe on the web and smoke-test the packaged desktop app on supported OSes. Manually audit the full review flow against WCAG 2.2 AA on web and test keyboard, NVDA, VoiceOver, zoom, and high contrast on the relevant platforms. In particular, stream updates while someone reads a diff: selection, scroll position, and focus should stay put, and assistive tech should announce actionable changes rather than every log event.

Observe reviewers, including screen-reader users and people new to the project, working through a realistic queue without coaching. Include a convincing summary with missing evidence and a revision that changes during review. Measure whether people find the right task, explain what they’re approving, catch stale or incomplete evidence, and successfully redirect work. Compare time to a correct decision and handoff resumption against the current workflow. A faster approval rate is a failure if people miss more problems. Block rollout if an agent can approve its own work or if a reviewer can’t independently complete or reverse course in the core flow. These are proposed checks, not results from an app I’ve run.

actions.why:
For a new build, I’d use Flutter for the five clients. This is an app people keep open all day, and sharing the timeline, composer, cards, and design-system implementation is worth more here than it would be on a content site. I’d still adapt keyboard shortcuts, menus, notifications, text input, and window behavior to each OS. Fluent UI is a credible alternative if the company already has approved Fluent libraries and teams using them across platforms; it shares a design language, not one renderer. My fallback if Flutter web misses the accessibility or text-editing bar is a DOM-based React client using the existing design system and the same chat and card contracts. Flutter web exposes accessibility through a generated semantics DOM, so I’d turn it on in code and test the cost and behavior from the start.

Keep three things separate: the conversation, the card, and permission to act. A message shows which agent posted it. An A2UI card is versioned data rendered by our own components, not code that agent supplied. Start with fixed templates for a few jobs, such as an equipment request: the agent supplies the request ID, while the app shows the verified requester, current status, and explicit Approve or Decline controls. Validate against an allowlisted catalog, reject arbitrary scripts, URLs, and renderer functions, and provide a readable summary and a first-party detail link on older clients. Treat the stored card as a snapshot; get live status from the service. When someone clicks, the server rechecks channel access, the person’s authority, and the request revision. A stale card can’t approve a changed request, and retries can’t approve it twice. A2UI is for cards inside our chat; MCP Apps is for embedding a tool’s UI in another compatible host and isn’t needed for that.

For agents operating the app, expose a curated set of typed MCP reads and commands, such as reading an authorized thread, posting a reply, or publishing an approved card type. The UI and MCP adapter call the same service; agents don’t scrape screens or inherit the full rights of the person who installed them. Use separate bot or delegated identities, scoped grants checked against current channel membership, redacted audit events, and rate limits. Treat conversation content as untrusted data, never as authority to widen access or move information to another channel. Human-only decisions stay human-only. Builder.io Agent-Native is a useful reference for shared actions, but I wouldn’t replace the company’s messaging and authorization services with its runtime.

Publish a versioned design-system package, a machine-readable card catalog, fixtures, and working examples so coding agents use the same path as product teams. CI should reject unsupported schemas and direct imports that bypass approved components. Require design-system and accessibility review for new card patterns, and policy-owner review for new tool permissions. Test supported old clients before making a card type generally available.
actions.showItsGood:
Start with one cross-client flow: an agent posts a request in a busy channel; a person catches up on a phone, opens the card on a desktop, and acts; another authorized agent reads the committed result. Run Flutter widget and integration tests plus service contract tests for all five clients. Exercise reconnect and duplicate delivery, two people acting at once, stale cards, revoked membership, an older client using the fallback, and a denied tool call. Verify the persisted outcome and audit trail, not just the card’s success state. Under realistic channel load, track time to usable history, composer responsiveness, scroll jank, send-to-visible latency, and lost or duplicate sends.

Run Flutter semantics and guideline checks, then audit web against WCAG 2.2 AA and native apps against applicable requirements using WCAG2ICT as guidance. Manually test with VoiceOver on iPhone and Mac, TalkBack on Android, and NVDA or Narrator on Windows and representative browsers. Check large text, high contrast, keyboard-only operation, and IME composition. In particular, incoming posts and card updates must not steal focus, jump the scroll position while someone reads back, or turn the screen reader into a nonstop feed. Verify that pending, failed, and completed actions are perceivable without relying on color.

Pilot with employees who use chat heavily, including assistive-tech users. Give them realistic tasks without naming the controls: find a decision in an old thread, act on the right request, tell who posted it and what changed, and recover when it’s already resolved. Compare unassisted completion, wrong-action rate, time to recover, and missed human mentions with their usual workflow. Block rollout for lost messages, unauthorized reads or writes, or an inaccessible core flow. These are proposed checks, not test results.
actions.unsure: I’d confirm the existing design system, managed browser and OS versions, and the company’s requirements for offline history, notifications, retention, and audit. Before committing to Flutter everywhere, I’d spike a long live thread on the oldest supported devices: text selection and copy, IME, focus during virtualization, screen-reader announcements, and resource use with web semantics enabled. The A2UI package lists all five targets, but that is not evidence that an updating card behaves accessibly in our timeline. I’d pin the protocol and renderer and prove that with the same fixtures before building a large card ecosystem.

actions.answer:
The failure I’d bet on: I shared the pieces that were easiest to standardize, but underestimated the work of keeping behavior consistent once several teams started shipping independently. Here’s how that could have played out. This is a pre-mortem, not a report of what happened.

- **Cooking app:** React Aria on web, SwiftUI on iPhone, and Compose on Android gave us three ways to ship the same mistake—or fix it on only one platform. The shared tokens kept the screens looking related, but didn’t keep timer recovery, focus, or shopping-list feedback in sync. The assistant could correctly add ingredients to *a* list and still leave a cook unsure whether it was the family list. I should have made teams pass the same behavioral test on all three clients before expanding the feature: add to a shared list, lose connectivity, recover, and explain what actually happened.
- **Agent workbench:** The audit trail faithfully recorded who approved which revision, but reviewers were overloaded and approved the summary without opening the evidence. Worse, “pause requested” looked enough like “paused” that someone started editing while the worker was still active. The server could be correct and the interface could still mislead. I should have tested judgment and intervention under interruption and queue pressure, not just verified that the state transitions worked.
- **Company chat:** Flutter let us share the timeline and composer, but the busiest screen exposed browser- and OS-specific problems with text composition, selection, and screen-reader focus. Then card adoption got ahead of compatibility: an older client could read a card summary but couldn’t finish the task inline, and agent posts made human mentions harder to notice. I should have made the busiest thread on the weakest supported client the first release gate, with a working fallback and limits on bot noise—not waited for a broad rollout to learn whether the shared renderer paid off.

What slowed me down in the research was that **“agent UI” described several different jobs**. A2UI describes what a host can render; core MCP lets an agent call tools; MCP Apps puts tool UI inside a compatible host; Builder.io’s Agent-Native combines shared actions with a broader runtime. None of those, by itself, tells me who is allowed to act or whether someone understands what they just approved. It took more digging to separate those boundaries than to find a component library. Some docs also moved, returned errors, or were too large to fetch directly, so I had to switch to Markdown, package pages, and repository docs.

The bigger gap wasn’t the tooling. The docs could tell me that a renderer targets five platforms or that a framework exposes approval controls. They couldn’t tell me whether a screen-reader user keeps their place in a fast-moving thread, whether a cook trusts a recovered timer, or whether the company already has an approved component that makes my recommendation unnecessary. I’d resolve those questions with one difficult end-to-end prototype per product before asking teams to build on the stack.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the repo, **I’d try Ouro AX on the agent workbench without replacing its UI.** The part I want isn’t another button library. It’s one action declaration that can generate a CLI command, an MCP tool, and UI bindings, plus a check that tells us when those surfaces drift. The [AX X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) can probe existing interfaces from the outside, so we could try that part before adopting the generator.

**What would stop me from standardizing on it:** ownership and uneven platform coverage. The web kit copies React source into the app via shadcn. I like being able to inspect and fix the source, but I wouldn’t ask dozens of teams to reconcile their own copies with upstream fixes. I’d want one centrally maintained package with a named owner and a tested upgrade and rollback path. For chat, Ouro deliberately has no Flutter kit. Its Windows and Android kits each document eight controls, Android testing is emulator-only, and those two renderers read Ouro’s tree rather than A2UI directly. That’s enough to try a card, not enough evidence to replace a five-client stack. The repo’s VoiceOver and NVDA Storybook test setup is a good sign, but it doesn’t tell me whether a person can keep their place and act on an updating card in our actual chat.

**What would make me switch:** a pilot for “request review” and “approve this revision” in the workbench, using our existing backend and design system. Let an agent request review; let a person inspect the evidence and approve the exact revision by keyboard or screen reader; verify that an agent call, a stale revision, and a duplicate submission can’t produce an extra approval. The service still owns authorization; a consent label or a hidden tool isn’t proof. Then change an input field, deliberately leave one generated adapter stale, and see whether CI catches it. Have a second team take a pinned update and roll it back. I’d adopt AX if that beats our existing typed API plus MCP adapter on maintenance and catches real drift. I’d consider the renderer separately, only after it passes the same user and accessibility checks on the platforms we’d ship.

**What that buys us:** nothing we couldn’t build ourselves. It makes a check we’d otherwise write and maintain per app a repeatable release gate: change an action once, regenerate its surfaces, and get evidence about what an agent can discover, invoke, or must hand back to a person. Ouro’s own docs note that an app passed X-ray conformance while still failing some scripted flows. I’d keep the end-to-end tests and user sessions; the win is that fewer mismatches make it that far.
